Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

derivations.claim: [The rotated pairs are orthonormal] By [F1] and [F2], $\langle e_{\theta},e_{\theta}\rangle=\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$, $\langle e_{\theta}^{\perp},e_{\theta}^{\perp}\rangle=\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1$ and $\langle e_{\theta},e_{\theta}^{\perp}\rangle=-\cos\theta\sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta=0$; hence $(e_{\theta},e_{\theta}^{\perp})$ is an orthonormal family of the two-dimensional space $V$, therefore an orthonormal basis of $V$.

[Overlaps and the cosine identity] By [F1] and [F2], $\langle e_{\theta},\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\cos\theta\cos\varphi+\sin\theta\sin\varphi=\cos(\theta-\varphi)$ and $\langle e_{\theta}^{\perp},\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=-\sin\theta\cos\varphi+\cos\theta\sin\varphi=\sin(\varphi-\theta)$. Then $\langle\psi_{\varphi},P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\langle\psi_{\varphi},\langle\psi_{\varphi},e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}\rangle=|\langle\psi_{\varphi},e_{\theta}\rangle|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$ because $\cos(\theta-\varphi)$ is real, and $\|P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=|\cos(\theta-\varphi)|^{2}\|e_{\theta}\|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$; similarly $\langle\psi_{\varphi},P_{\theta}^{\perp}\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\sin^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$. This is (b).

[The projections are orthogonal projections] For $x\in V$, $P_{\theta}x=\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}$, so $P_{\theta}(P_{\theta}x)=\langle\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta},e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}=\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle\langle e_{\theta},e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}=P_{\theta}x$ by [F1] and step 1.1: $P_{\theta}^{2}=P_{\theta}$. For the adjoint, $\langle P_{\theta}x,y\rangle=\langle\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta},y\rangle=\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle\langle e_{\theta},y\rangle=\langle x,\langle y,e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}\rangle=\langle x,P_{\theta}y\rangle$ for all $x,y$, so $P_{\theta}^{*}=P_{\theta}$; the same computation with $e_{\theta}^{\perp}$ in place of $e_{\theta}$ gives $P_{\theta}^{\perp\,2}=P_{\theta}^{\perp}=P_{\theta}^{\perp\,*}$. By [F4] both are the orthogonal projections onto their ranges $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}$ and $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}$.

[Complementarity] By step 1.1 and [F3] applied to the orthonormal basis $(e_{\theta},e_{\theta}^{\perp})$, every $x\in V$ satisfies $x=\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}+\langle x,e_{\theta}^{\perp}\rangle e_{\theta}^{\perp}=P_{\theta}x+P_{\theta}^{\perp}x$; hence $P_{\theta}+P_{\theta}^{\perp}=I$. Applying $P_{\theta}$ to the same expansion and using $P_{\theta}e_{\theta}^{\perp}=\langle e_{\theta}^{\perp},e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}=0$ gives $P_{\theta}P_{\theta}^{\perp}=0$, and likewise $P_{\theta}^{\perp}P_{\theta}=0$. Since $P_{\theta}=I-P_{\theta}^{\perp}$ and $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}\cap\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}=\{0\}$ by orthogonality of the nonzero vectors $e_{\theta},e_{\theta}^{\perp}$, the eigenspace of $P_{\theta}$ at eigenvalue $1$ is $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}$ and at eigenvalue $0$ is $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}$; this proves (a) and (d).

[Periodicity and phase invariance] Since $e_{\theta+\pi}=-e_{\theta}$ and $e_{\theta+\pi/2}=e_{\theta}^{\perp}$, the identities $P_{\theta+\pi}=P_{\theta}$ and $P_{\theta+\pi/2}=P_{\theta}^{\perp}$ follow from the definition of $P_{\theta}$ and [F1]; in particular $P_{\theta}$ is $2\pi$-periodic. For $z\ne0$ and the unit vector $\psi_{\varphi}$ one has $\|z\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=|z|^{2}$, and $P_{\theta}(z\psi_{\varphi})=zP_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}$ by linearity of $x\mapsto\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle$ in the first argument of [F1]; hence $\|P_{\theta}(z\psi_{\varphi})\|^{2}/\|z\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=\|P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$ by step 1.2. This proves (c) and completes the proof.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space with $\mu(X)>0$, let $m:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and finite $\mu$-almost everywhere, and on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^{2}(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) let
$$D(M_{m})=\Bigl\{f\in H:\int_{X}|m|^{2}|f|^{2}\,d\mu<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad M_{m}f=mf .$$
Then:

(a) $M_{m}$ is self-adjoint on $D(M_{m})$ ([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]] clause (a)).

(b) The assignment $E(B):=M_{\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}}$ on Borel sets $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a regular projection-valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and for a unit vector $\psi\in H$
$$\|E(B)\psi\|^{2}=\int_{m^{-1}(B)}|\psi|^{2}\,d\mu .$$

(c) The operator identity $\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)=M_{m}$ holds with domain $D(M_{m})$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); consequently $E$ is the spectral projection-valued measure of $M_{m}$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]).

(d) $E(B)=0$ if and only if $\mu(m^{-1}(B))=0$, and the spectrum $\sigma(M_{m})$ equals the essential range of $m$:
$$\sigma(M_{m})=\{\,t\in\mathbb R:\mu(m^{-1}(t-\varepsilon,t+\varepsilon))>0\ \text{for every}\ \varepsilon>0\,\}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$
on the complex Hilbert space $H$ and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be $\Sigma$-measurable. Then the
operator $f(E)$ of [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]] is densely defined
and closed, and it is normal, in the sense $D(f(E))=D(f(E)^*)$ and equal norms for the operator and its adjoint; in particular $D(f(E))=D(\overline f(E))$ and
$\|f(E)x\|=\|\overline f(E)x\|$ for all such $x$. Moreover
$$\|f(E)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x,\qquad \langle x,f(E)x\rangle=\int\overline f\,dE_x\qquad(x\in D(f(E))),$$
and $(f(E))^*=\overline f(E)$; in particular $f(E)$ is self-adjoint whenever
$f$ takes real values. Finally, if $(g_n)$ are bounded $\Sigma$-measurable functions with
$|g_n|\le C|f|$ pointwise and $g_n\to f$ pointwise, then $g_n(E)x\to f(E)x$
for every $x\in D(f(E))$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$
and let $f : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R$ be Lebesgue measurable.
Then its graph
$$\Gamma_f := \{(x,t) \in \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R : t=f(x)\}$$
is Lebesgue measurable and has $(n+1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.

set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

derivations.claim: [Restriction of the spectral measure] Let $m$ be one of the two displayed functions; both are real, measurable and finite-valued. By [F4] the multiplier $M_{m}$ commutes with $M_{\Pi}$, so $E(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}}$ (componentwise) commutes with $M_{\Pi}$ for every Borel set $B$ and therefore maps $\mathfrak h$ into itself: for $f\in\mathfrak h$ one has $E(B)f=\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}f\in\mathfrak h$ because transversality holds pointwise. Thus $E_{\mathfrak h}(B):=E(B)|_{\mathfrak h}$ is a family of projections on $\mathfrak h$ with $E_{\mathfrak h}(B)^{2}=E_{\mathfrak h}(B)=E_{\mathfrak h}(B)^{*}$, $E_{\mathfrak h}(\varnothing)=0$, $E_{\mathfrak h}(\mathbb R)=\mathrm{id}_{\mathfrak h}$, and $\sigma$-additivity and strong convergence inherited from $E$; hence $E_{\mathfrak h}$ is a projection-valued measure on $\mathfrak h$.

[No eigenvalues] Let $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and let $f\in D(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h})$ satisfy $M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}f=\lambda f$, that is $m(k)f(k)=\lambda f(k)$ for almost every $k$. Then $f=0$ almost everywhere on $\{k:m(k)\ne\lambda\}$, so $f$ is supported in $N_{\lambda}:=\{k:m(k)=\lambda\}$ up to a null set. For $m=\hbar k_{j}$ the set $N_{\lambda}$ is null by [F5]; for $m=\hbar c|k|$ it is null by [F6]. In both cases $f=0$ almost everywhere, hence $f=0$ in $L^{2}$. This proves (c).

[The restricted integral is the restricted multiplier] By [F3] applied to $E_{\mathfrak h}$ and the real function $\lambda\mapsto\lambda$ the operator $A:=\int\lambda\,dE_{\mathfrak h}(\lambda)$ is self-adjoint with domain $\{f\in\mathfrak h:\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{\mathfrak h,f}(\lambda)<\infty\}$. For every $g\in\mathfrak h$ and Borel $B$ we have $\langle E_{\mathfrak h}(B)g,g\rangle=\int_{m^{-1}(B)}\|g(k)\|^{2}\,d^{3}k$: the scalar statements of [F2] applied to the three components of $g$ combine by sesquilinearity, and the unit case extends by scaling in $g$, so the scalar measure $E_{\mathfrak h,g}$ is the push-forward of $\|g\|^{2}\,d^{3}k$ under $k\mapsto m(k)$; hence $\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{\mathfrak h,f}(\lambda)=\int m(k)^{2}\|f(k)\|^{2}\,d^{3}k$ by the change-of-variables formula for a push-forward measure against the Borel function $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{2}$, the two sides agreeing on indicators of Borel sets and extending by linearity and monotone convergence. Therefore $D(A)=\{f\in\mathfrak h:\int m^{2}\|f\|^{2}\,d^{3}k<\infty\}=D(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h})$.

[Identification on the domain] Let $f\in D(A)$ and put $m_{n}:=m\mathbf 1_{\{|m|\le n\}}$ for $n\ge1$; then $|m_{n}|\le|m|$ and $m_{n}\to m$ pointwise, so [F3] gives $m_{n}(E_{\mathfrak h})f\to Af$. For $g\in\mathfrak h$ the bounded operator $m_{n}(E_{\mathfrak h})$ satisfies $\langle m_{n}(E_{\mathfrak h})g,g\rangle=\int m_{n}\,dE_{\mathfrak h,g}=\int m_{n}(k)\|g(k)\|^{2}\,d^{3}k=\langle m_{n}g,g\rangle$ by the push-forward description of step 2.1; both operators are bounded and self-adjoint and their quadratic forms agree, so $m_{n}(E_{\mathfrak h})=M_{m_{n}}|_{\mathfrak h}$: the bounded functional calculus of the restricted multiplier is multiplication by $m_{n}$. The convergence $m_{n}f\to mf$ in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{3})$ holds by dominated convergence, since $\|m_{n}f-mf\|^{2}\le4m^{2}\|f\|^{2}$ is integrable under $f\in D(A)$; its limit $mf$ lies in $\mathfrak h$ because transversality is preserved pointwise, with no assertion that $mf$ belongs to $D(A)$; that stronger assertion would require $m^2f\in L^2$. Hence $Af=mf=M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}f$ for every $f\in D(A)$; conversely if $f\in D(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h})$ then $\int m^{2}\|f\|^{2}=\|mf\|^{2}<\infty$, so $f\in D(A)$. Therefore $A=M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}$ with the displayed domain, and (a) and (b) follow.

[Positive variance] Let $f\in\mathfrak h$ be a unit vector in $D(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h})$ and put $\mu:=\langle M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}f,f\rangle$, a real number because $M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}$ is self-adjoint. Then $$\|M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}f\|^{2}-\langle M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}f,f\rangle^{2}=\|(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}-\mu I)f\|^{2}\ge0,$$ and equality holds exactly when $(M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}-\mu I)f=0$, that is when $f$ is an eigenvector of $M_{m}^{\mathfrak h}$ with eigenvalue $\mu$. By step 1.2 no nonzero eigenvector exists, so the left-hand side is strictly positive. This proves (d) and completes the proof.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Let
$H^{\otimes 0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes 1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(n+1)}:=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$ be the completed tensor
powers with elementary tensors $u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_n$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); for $n\ge 1$ let
$P_+^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ be the symmetric projection of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] and set
$P_+^{(0)}:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$. Write $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for
its range and define

$$F(H):=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$

Then:

(a) for $\psi,\varphi\in F(H)$ the scalar series
$\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ converges absolutely and
defines a sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument, with respect to
which $F(H)$ is a complex vector space with inner product
$\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$
([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]],
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]]);

(b) $(F(H),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is a Hilbert space, i.e. the induced norm
is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]);

(c) the vacuum vector $\Omega:=(1,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies $\|\Omega\|=1$, and the
finite-particle space
$F_0:=\{\psi\in F(H):\psi_n=0\ \text{for all but finitely many }n\}$ is a dense
linear subspace of $F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]]);

(d) for every $n$ the map
$\iota_n:\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\to F(H)$,
$\iota_n(u):=(0,\dots,0,u,0,\dots)$ (entry in coordinate $n$) is a linear
isometry of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ onto the closed subspace of vectors
supported in coordinate $n$;

(e) if $H$ admits a countable complete orthonormal family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$, $I$ at most countable
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
then $F(H)$ is separable ([[def-separable-space]]);

(f) *direct sums of self-adjoint operators*: if for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
including $n=0$, a self-adjoint operator $T_n$ on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with domain
$D(T_n)\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is given (so $T_0$ is a
self-adjoint operator on $\mathbb C$),
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]), and

$$D(T):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (T\psi)_n:=T_n\psi_n,$$

then $T$ is self-adjoint and $D(T)$ is dense; if in addition every $T_n$ is
bounded with $\sup_{n}\|T_n\|<\infty$, then $T$ is bounded with
$\|T\|=\sup_n\|T_n\|$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

No physical interpretation of $F(H)$, of the tensor powers or of the direct-sum
operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers
$H^{\otimes n}$ and symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$ as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]], so that
$$F(H)=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)},\ \sum_n\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}$$
is a Hilbert space. For $n\in\mathbb N$ define
$$\Pi_n:F(H)\to F(H),\qquad \Pi_n\psi:=(0,\dots,0,\psi_n,0,\dots)$$
(the entry $\psi_n$ in coordinate $n$ and $0$ in all other coordinates). Then:

(a) each $\Pi_n$ is a bounded linear operator with
$\|\Pi_n\psi\|=\|\psi_n\|$ and $\|\Pi_n\|\le1$; it satisfies
$\Pi_n^2=\Pi_n$, $\Pi_n^*=\Pi_n$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]), and
$\Pi_n$ is the Hilbert orthogonal projection of $F(H)$ onto the closed subspace
$\iota_n(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)})$ of vectors supported in coordinate $n$
([[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]);

(b) $\Pi_n\Pi_m=0$ for $n\ne m$, so the ranges are pairwise orthogonal and
$\|\Pi_n\|=1$ whenever $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ne\{0\}$ (which holds for
every $n$ when $H\ne\{0\}$);

(c) for every $\psi\in F(H)$ the series $\sum_{n}\Pi_n\psi$ converges in norm to
$\psi$, the expansion is orthogonal,
$$\psi=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\Pi_n\psi,\qquad \|\psi\|^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\Pi_n\psi\|^2,$$
and the partial sums $\sum_{n\le N}\Pi_n$ converge to the identity in the strong
operator topology, i.e. $\bigl\|\psi-\sum_{n\le N}\Pi_n\psi\bigr\|\to0$ for
every $\psi\in F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]);

(d) $\Pi_n=0$ as an operator if and only if
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\{0\}$; for $H\ne\{0\}$ no $\Pi_n$ vanishes.

No physical interpretation of the Fock space or of its sectors is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space with completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric
projections $P_+^{(n)}$ and Fock space $F(H)$ as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]]. Define the
number operator by
$$D(N):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}n^2\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (N\psi)_n:=n\psi_n .$$
Then:

(a) $N$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $F(H)$ with the displayed
domain; $N\ge0$ in the sense that $\langle N\psi,\psi\rangle\ge0$ for
$\psi\in D(N)$, $N\Omega=0$, and $F_0$ is a core for $N$
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(b) for every $n$, every nonzero $u\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ satisfies
$N\iota_n(u)=n\,\iota_n(u)$, and for $H\ne\{0\}$ the spectrum of $N$ is
$\sigma(N)=\mathbb N$;

(c) for $f\in H$ and $\psi\in F_0$ the core operators of
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]] satisfy
$$N S_+(f)\psi-S_+(f)N\psi=S_+(f)\psi,\qquad N S_-(f)\psi-S_-(f)N\psi=-S_-(f)\psi ;$$

(d) $D(N)\subseteq D_1:=\{\psi:\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, and for every
$\psi\in D(N)$,
$$\|N\psi\|^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}n^2\|\psi_n\|^2,\qquad \langle N\psi,\psi\rangle=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}n\|\psi_n\|^2 .$$

No physical interpretation of $N$, and no assertion about particle number
measurement, is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers
$H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$, contraction maps
$\Psi_f^{(n)}$, Fock space $F(H)$ and core operators $S_\pm(f)$ on the
finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For $f\in H$
define
$$D(A_+(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n)\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\ (A_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$
$$D(A_-(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1}).$$
Put $D_1:=\{\psi\in F(H):\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$. Then:

(a) $A_+(f)$ and $A_-(f)$ are well-defined linear operators on $F(H)$ with the
displayed domains, and they are the closure and the adjoint of the core operator:
$$A_+(f)=\overline{S_+(f)}=S_-(f)^*,\qquad A_-(f)=S_+(f)^*=\overline{S_-(f)}$$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(b) both $A_\pm(f)$ are closed, densely defined and satisfy
$A_+(f)^*=A_-(f)$, $A_-(f)^*=A_+(f)$; in particular $F_0\subseteq D_1\subseteq D(A_\pm(f))$;

(c) for every $\psi\in D_1$, $\|A_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$ and
$\|A_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$, where
$\|\psi\|_1^2=\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2$;

(d) for every $g\in H$ and $\psi\in D_1$ the identity
$$\|A_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2$$
holds.

No boundedness of $A_\pm(f)$ on $F(H)$, no self-adjointness of $A_\pm(f)$, and
no physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with
completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$,
Fock space $F(H)$ and finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fock-sector-projections]].

(a) *Contraction map.* For every $f\in H$ and $n\ge0$ there is a unique bounded
linear map $\Psi_f^{(n)}:H^{\otimes(n+1)}\to H^{\otimes n}$ with
$$\langle\varphi,\Psi_f^{(n)}\chi\rangle=\langle f\otimes\varphi,\chi\rangle \qquad(\varphi\in H^{\otimes n},\ \chi\in H^{\otimes(n+1)})$$
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]); it satisfies
$\|\Psi_f^{(n)}\|\le\|f\|$,
$\Psi_f^{(n)}(u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1})=\langle u_1,f\rangle\,u_2\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1}$
on elementary tensors, $\Psi_f^{(n)}(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n+1)})\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$,
and the map $f\mapsto\Psi_f^{(n)}$ is conjugate-linear.

(b) *Creation and annihilation on the core.* Define, for $f\in H$ and
$\psi\in F_0$,
$$(S_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\quad (S_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$
$$(S_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\ (n\ge0).$$
Then $S_+(f)\psi,S_-(f)\psi\in F_0$; $S_+(f)$ is linear in $f$ and
$S_-(f)$ is conjugate-linear in $f$; and with
$\|\psi\|_1^2:=\sum_{n}\bigl(n+1\bigr)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for $\psi\in F_0$,
$$\|S_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1,\qquad \|S_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1.$$

(c) *Adjoint relation.* $\langle S_+(f)\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,S_-(f)\psi\rangle$
for all $f\in H$ and $\varphi,\psi\in F_0$
([[def-operator-norm]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

(d) *Canonical commutation relation.* For all $f,g\in H$ and $\psi\in F_0$,
$$S_-(f)S_+(g)\psi-S_+(g)S_-(f)\psi=\langle g,f\rangle\,\psi,$$
and consequently
$$\|S_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|S_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2.$$

Neither $S_+(f)$ nor $S_-(f)$ is asserted to be bounded on $F(H)$, and no
physical interpretation (particle creation, radiation or measurement) is
asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\mathbb H:=\mathbb C$ with its standard inner product (linear in the first
argument), let $F(\mathbb C)$ be its Fock space as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]], let
$e_n\in F(\mathbb C)$ be the unit vector supported in coordinate $n$ (so
$(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $F(\mathbb C)$),
let $N$ be the number operator and let $A_\pm(1)$ be the maximal creation and
annihilation operators of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-closed-adjoint-sector-domains]] for the vector
$1\in\mathbb C$. Then:

(a) *oscillator coefficients*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$A_+(1)e_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,e_{n+1},\qquad A_-(1)e_n=\sqrt n\,e_{n-1}\ (n\ge1),\qquad A_-(1)e_0=0;$$

(b) *coherent vectors*: for every $z\in\mathbb C$ the series
$$\psi_z:=e^{-|z|^2/2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\frac{z^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\,e_n$$
converges absolutely in $F(\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]),
$\|\psi_z\|=1$, $\psi_z\in D(A_-(1))$ with
$$A_-(1)\psi_z=z\,\psi_z,$$
and for all $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$\langle\psi_z,\psi_w\rangle=e^{-(|z|^2+|w|^2)/2+z\overline w};$$

(c) *number law*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$\bigl|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle\bigr|^2=e^{-|z|^2}\frac{|z|^{2n}}{n!},$$
and $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle|^2=1$.

The numbers in (c) are squared moduli of overlaps of unit vectors; identifying
them with outcome probabilities of a number measurement requires a separately
adopted measurement postulate, and no such physical claim is made here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, the Axiom of Dependent Choice and the
Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a parameter $\alpha>0$, define the transverse
subspace
$$\mathfrak h:=\Bigl\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):\ k\cdot f(k)=0\ \text{for a.e. }k\Bigr\}$$
with the $L^2$ inner product, define the bounded multiplier-valued function
$\Pi(k):=\mathrm{id}-|k|^{-2}kk^{\mathsf T}$ for $k\ne0$ and $\Pi(0):=0$, and let
$M_\Pi$ be multiplication by $\Pi$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Write
$\varepsilon(k):=\alpha|k|$ and let $M_\varepsilon$ be multiplication by
$\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}:=M_\varepsilon|_{\mathfrak h}$.
Let $F(\mathfrak h)$ be the Fock space of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] with sectors
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and for $n\ge1$ define
$$T_n\psi:=\varepsilon_n\psi,\quad \varepsilon_n(k_1,\dots,k_n):=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha|k_i|,\qquad D(T_n):=\{\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}:\varepsilon_n\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\},$$
and $T_0:=0$ on $\mathbb C$. Finally put
$$H_f:=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T_n,\qquad D(H_f):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(\mathfrak h):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\text{ for every }n,\ \sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$
Then:

(a) $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_\Pi$ is a closed separable subspace of
$L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, invariant under $M_\varepsilon$, and
$\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on
$\mathfrak h$ with $D(\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h})=\{f\in\mathfrak h:\varepsilon f\in\mathfrak h\}$
([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]],
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]);

(b) each $T_n$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with the displayed domain
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]],
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]);

(c) $H_f$ is self-adjoint and positive with domain $D(H_f)$; it commutes with
every sector projection $\Pi_n$ (i.e. $T_n$ maps its sector into itself);

(d) for every $\beta>0$ the bounded operator $e^{-\beta H_f}$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]) is not compact and in particular not trace
class ([[def-compact-linear-operator]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]); more
precisely its restriction to the one-particle sector equals the multiplication
operator $M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}$ on $\mathfrak h$, which is not compact, and
the restriction of a compact operator to a closed invariant subspace is compact.

The identification of $\mathfrak h$, $\varepsilon$ and $H_f$ with physical
transverse photons in a chosen frame is a separate model assumption and is not
asserted here; no thermal interpretation of $e^{-\beta H_f}$ is claimed either.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

derivations.claim: [The powers of $\varphi$ are orthonormal sector vectors] For $n\ge0$ put $\Phi_n:=\varphi^{\otimes n}$, with $\Phi_0:=1$. By [F2] with $u=\varphi$ and $\|\varphi\|=1$ one has $\|\Phi_n\|=1$ for every $n$, $P_+^{(n)}\Phi_n=\Phi_n$, and $\langle\Phi_n,\Phi_n\rangle=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\langle\varphi,\varphi\rangle=1$; for $m\ne n$ the pairing $\langle\Phi_m,\Phi_n\rangle$ vanishes because $\Phi_m$ is supported in the direct-sum coordinate $m$ and $\Phi_n$ in coordinate $n$, and the inner product of $F(H)$ is the sum of the coordinate pairings by [F1]. Hence $(\Phi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is an orthonormal family with $\Phi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for every $n$.

[The isometry] Define $U_\varphi$ on the finite linear span of $(e_n)$ by $U_\varphi e_n=\Phi_n$ and extend by linearity; by step 1.1, $\|U_\varphi\psi\|^{2}=\sum_n|\psi_n|^{2}=\|\psi\|^{2}$ for every finite combination, so $U_\varphi$ is isometric on the dense finite-particle subspace $F_0(\mathbb C)$ of [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] clause (c) and extends uniquely to an isometry $U_\varphi:F(\mathbb C)\to F(H)$ with the same norm identity for all $\psi\in F(\mathbb C)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]). Its range is the closed linear span of $(\Phi_n)$, since an isometry maps the closed span of an orthonormal family onto the closed span of its image and the image family is orthonormal; this proves (a).

[Ladder transfer on the exact domains] Write $\psi=\sum_n\psi_ne_n$. By [F4] and [F5], $\psi\in D(A_+(1))$ exactly when $\sum_n(n+1)|\psi_n|^2<\infty$, while $\psi\in D(A_-(1))$ exactly when $\sum_n(n+1)|\psi_{n+1}|^2=\sum_{m\ge1}m|\psi_m|^2<\infty$. For the unit mode $\varphi$, [F2] gives $P_+^{(n+1)}(\varphi\otimes\psi_n\Phi_n)=\psi_n\Phi_{n+1}$ and [F4] gives $\Psi_\varphi^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1}\Phi_{n+1})=\psi_{n+1}\Phi_n$. Therefore the two exact domain sums for $U_\varphi\psi$ equal the respective scalar sums, without any extra weighted output assumption. On these domains, $(A_+(\varphi)U_\varphi\psi)_n=\sqrt n\psi_{n-1}\Phi_n=(U_\varphi A_+(1)\psi)_n$ for $n\ge1$, with zero vacuum coordinate, and $(A_-(\varphi)U_\varphi\psi)_n=\sqrt{n+1}\psi_{n+1}\Phi_n=(U_\varphi A_-(1)\psi)_n$. This proves (c), including its coherent-vector specialization by [F5].

[Energy expectation] Assume now $H=\mathfrak h$ and $\varphi$ unit with $\varepsilon\varphi\in\mathfrak h$; write $\bar\varepsilon:=\langle\varepsilon\varphi,\varphi\rangle$. For fixed $n$, $\Phi_n=\varphi^{\otimes n}\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ and, by [F6], $T_n\Phi_n=\varepsilon_n\Phi_n$; using the Euclidean identification and the symmetry of $\varepsilon_n$ under the permutation action, the iterated $L^{2}$ integral gives $$\langle T_n\Phi_n,\Phi_n\rangle=\int_{(\mathbb R^{3})^{n}}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varepsilon(k_i)\Bigr)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\|\varphi(k_i)\|_{\mathbb C^{3}}^{2}\,d^{3}k_1\cdots d^{3}k_n=n\,\bar\varepsilon\,\|\varphi\|^{2(n-1)}=n\,\bar\varepsilon,$$ each of the $n$ summands contributing the same product $\bar\varepsilon\|\varphi\|^{2(n-1)}$ by Tonelli's theorem, the product measure being $\sigma$-finite and the integrand nonnegative; this is finite because $\varepsilon\varphi\in L^{2}$ and $\varphi\in L^{2}$ give $\int\varepsilon\|\varphi\|^{2}\le\|\varepsilon\varphi\|\,\|\varphi\|<\infty$. The actual domain is also justified: by the triangle inequality on the product space, $\|T_n\Phi_n\|\le n\|\varepsilon\varphi\|$, since each factor multiplier has that norm and all other factors have norm one. Hence $\sum_n|\psi_n|^2\|T_n\Phi_n\|^2\le\|\varepsilon\varphi\|^2\sum_n n^2|\psi_n|^2<\infty$, so $U_\varphi\psi\in D(H_f)$ and its finite-sector truncations converge in the graph norm: the squared graph-tail norms are the tails of these two convergent nonnegative series. Therefore for a finite combination the sector-diagonal form of $H_f$ (clause (c) of [F6]) gives $\langle H_fU_\varphi\psi,U_\varphi\psi\rangle=\sum_n|\psi_n|^{2}\,n\bar\varepsilon$; the general case $\sum_nn^{2}|\psi_n|^{2}<\infty$ follows by approximation with truncations in the graph norm of $H_f$ (both sides are continuous under this approximation, the left because $H_f$ is closed and self-adjoint, the right by dominated convergence). This proves the first two displays of (d).

[Sector and number transfer] For $\psi=\sum_m\psi_me_m$ in the dense span and fixed $n$, $\Pi_nU_\varphi\psi=\psi_n\Phi_n=U_\varphi(\psi_ne_n)=U_\varphi\Pi_n'\psi$; since both sides are bounded in $\psi$ and the span is dense, the identity extends to all $\psi\in F(\mathbb C)$, and the norm identity is step 2.1. For $\psi\in F(\mathbb C)$ the coefficient vector of $U_\varphi\psi$ is again $(\psi_n)$, so $\sum_nn^{2}\|(U_\varphi\psi)_n\|^{2}=\sum_nn^{2}|\psi_n|^{2}$: $U_\varphi\psi\in D(N)$ exactly when $\psi\in D(N')$, and then $(NU_\varphi\psi)_n=n\psi_n\Phi_n=(U_\varphi N'\psi)_n$ for every $n$ by [F3]. This proves (b).

[Spectral second moment and literal square domain] For $\varphi\in D(\varepsilon)$, expand $\varepsilon_n^2=\sum_i\varepsilon(k_i)^2+\sum_{i\ne j}\varepsilon(k_i)\varepsilon(k_j)$ and integrate against $\prod_i\|\varphi(k_i)\|^2$. Tonelli gives $\|T_n\Phi_n\|^2=n\|\varepsilon\varphi\|^2+n(n-1)\bar\varepsilon^2$, finite by the stated domain and Cauchy-Schwarz. This is the spectral second moment and requires no $T_n^2\Phi_n$. If $\varphi\in D(\varepsilon^2)$, the inequality $(\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon(k_i))^4\le n^3\sum_i\varepsilon(k_i)^4$ gives $\|T_n^2\Phi_n\|^2\le n^4\|\varepsilon^2\varphi\|^2<\infty$, so $\Phi_n\in D(T_n^2)$; self-adjointness then gives $\langle T_n^2\Phi_n,\Phi_n\rangle=\|T_n\Phi_n\|^2$, exactly the original operator-square display. The vacuum has energy zero and all its moments vanish, handled separately when $n=0$.

Let $V$ be a two-dimensional complex inner product space with inner product
linear in the first argument ([[def-inner-product-space]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), and let $(e_{1},e_{2})$ be an
orthonormal basis of $V$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
For $\theta\in\mathbb R$ put
$$e_{\theta}:=\cos\theta\,e_{1}+\sin\theta\,e_{2},\qquad e_{\theta}^{\perp}:=-\sin\theta\,e_{1}+\cos\theta\,e_{2},$$
and for $x\in V$ define
$$P_{\theta}x:=\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle\,e_{\theta},\qquad P_{\theta}^{\perp}x:=\langle x,e_{\theta}^{\perp}\rangle\,e_{\theta}^{\perp}.$$
Then:

(a) for every $\theta$ the maps $P_{\theta}$ and $P_{\theta}^{\perp}$ are
orthogonal projections on $V$ with ranges $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}$ and
$\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}$ ([[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]],
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]]), one has
$P_{\theta}+P_{\theta}^{\perp}=I$ and $P_{\theta}P_{\theta}^{\perp}=0$, and
$$P_{\theta}P_{\theta}=P_{\theta}=P_{\theta}^{*},\qquad P_{\theta}P_{\theta}^{\perp}=P_{\theta}^{\perp}P_{\theta}=0;$$

(b) for all real $\varphi,\theta$ the unit vectors
$\psi_{\varphi}:=\cos\varphi\,e_{1}+\sin\varphi\,e_{2}$ satisfy
$$\langle e_{\theta},\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\cos(\theta-\varphi),\qquad \langle\psi_{\varphi},P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\|P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=|\langle e_{\theta},\psi_{\varphi}\rangle|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi),$$
and $\langle\psi_{\varphi},P_{\theta}^{\perp}\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\sin^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$;

(c) the assignments $\theta\mapsto P_{\theta}$ and $\theta\mapsto
P_{\theta}^{\perp}$ are $2\pi$-periodic, $P_{\theta+\pi}=P_{\theta}$ and
$P_{\theta+\pi/2}=P_{\theta}^{\perp}$, and for every $z\in\mathbb C$ and
$x\in V$ one has $P_{\theta}(zx)=zP_{\theta}x$ and
$\|P_{\theta}(z\psi_{\varphi})\|^{2}/\|z\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$
whenever $z\ne0$; in particular the number $\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$ depends
only on the ray $[\psi_{\varphi}]$, not on the representative;

(d) the pair $(P_{\theta},P_{\theta}^{\perp})$ is a two-element family of
mutually orthogonal projections on $V$ with $P_{\theta}+P_{\theta}^{\perp}=I$,
the spectral values $1$ and $0$ of the bounded self-adjoint operator
$P_{\theta}$ have projections $P_{\theta}$ and $P_{\theta}^{\perp}$,
respectively. These two alternatives may be labelled $+1$ and $-1$ in a
declared analyser; those labels are not the spectral values of $P_{\theta}$.
The eigenspace of $P_{\theta}$ at eigenvalue $1$ is
$\mathbb Ce_{\theta}$ and the eigenspace at eigenvalue $0$ is
$\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}$.

No physical interpretation of $V$, of the pair $(e_{1},e_{2})$ or of the
projections $P_{\theta}$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Adopt the state postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] (P1), the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) and the ideal conditional-measurement postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-ideal-conditional-measurement]] (P3) for the declared system, whose state space is $D(H)$ for the assigned nonzero separable complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]). Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis of the cited mathematics. The following vocabulary is used by this page.

**(a) Declared ideal sharp measurement.** A **declared ideal sharp measurement** of the system is a finite or countably infinite family $(P_{a})_{a\in A}$ of bounded orthogonal projections on $H$ ([[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]) that are **mutually orthogonal**, $P_{a}P_{b}=0$ for $a\ne b$, and whose **strong sum** is the identity,
$$\sum_{a\in A}P_{a}x=x\qquad(x\in H).$$
The index $a$ is the **outcome label** and the family $(P_{a})_{a\in A}$ is the **outcome structure** of the declared measurement; it is part of the declared apparatus model, not a quantity computed from the state. This is clause (i) of P3.

**(b) The Lueders instrument of a declared ideal sharp measurement.** For a preparation $\rho$ the **outcome probabilities** are
$$p_{a}:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_{a})\ge0,\qquad \sum_{a}p_{a}=1,$$
and for a pure preparation of the unit ray $[\psi]$ they are $p_{a}=\|P_{a}\psi\|^{2}$ (clause (ii) of P3, read with the outcome law of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]). If $p_{a}>0$ the **conditional state** after the outcome $a$ is the selective Lueders update
$$\rho_{a}:=\frac{P_{a}\rho P_{a}}{p_{a}};$$
it is a state with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{a}P_{a})=1$ and $P_{a}\rho_{a}P_{a}=\rho_{a}$ ([[lem-nrqm-measurement-selective-luders-update]], clause (iii) of P3). If the outcomes are recorded but not selected, the **discarded-outcome state** is
$$\Phi(\rho):=\sum_{a\in A}P_{a}\rho P_{a},$$
the trace-norm convergent series of [[lem-nrqm-measurement-nonselective-luders-map]]; it is a state with $\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{a:p_{a}>0}p_{a}\rho_{a}$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(\rho)P_{a})=p_{a}$ (clause (iv) of P3).

**(c) Declared ideal filter.** A **declared ideal filter** is a declared ideal sharp measurement with exactly two outcomes $a=1,2$: the filter **passes** the component in the range of $P_{1}$ and **blocks** the component in the range of $P_{2}=I-P_{1}$. Repeated use of the filter in series means the sequential application of the conditional updates of clause (b).

**(d) Declared instrument.** A **declared finite or countable instrument** for an outcome set $A$ consists of a finite or countable family $(M_{a,r})_{\substack{a\in A\\r\in R_{a}}}$ of bounded operators on $H$ with
$$\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{r\in R_{a}}M_{a,r}^{*}M_{a,r}=I$$
in the strong sense ([[lem-nrqm-composites-countable-kraus-normalization]]), the **effects**
$$F_{a}:=\sum_{r\in R_{a}}M_{a,r}^{*}M_{a,r},$$
where each subseries converges strongly, independently of its enumeration. An **effect** on general $H$ is a bounded self-adjoint operator $F$ with $0\le\langle Fx,x\rangle\le\|x\|^2$ for all $x\in H$; the **order** $F\le G$ means $\langle(G-F)x,x\rangle\ge0$ for all $x$. Here $\langle F_a x,x\rangle=\sum_r\|M_{a,r}x\|^2\le\|x\|^2$, so $0\le F_a\le I$. In particular the positive partial sums $S_N$ of any subseries are contractions and have convergent quadratic forms; for a positive tail $D=S_N-S_m$, the positive-form Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives $\|Dx\|^2\le\langle Dx,x\rangle$, so $S_Nx$ is Cauchy and its limit defines $F_a$. The **outcome probabilities** are $p_{a}:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_{a})$ of clause (iv) of P2, the **conditional updates**
$$\rho\longmapsto\frac{1}{p_{a}}\sum_{r\in R_{a}}M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^{*}\qquad(p_{a}>0),$$
and the **discarded-outcome map** $\rho\mapsto\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^{*}$. The family $(M_{a,r})$, called the **Kraus family** of the instrument, is part of the declared apparatus model. The effects $(F_{a})$ alone do not determine the conditional updates: distinct normalized Kraus families can share the same effects while defining different updates ([[lem-nrqm-composites-finite-effects-and-instruments]] clause (d); clause (v) of P3). More generally, on a specified measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$, a **declared abstract instrument** is a map $J:\Sigma\to\mathcal B(\mathcal S_{1}(H))$ into bounded complex-linear maps of trace-class operators satisfying: each $J_B$ is completely positive, meaning every finite matrix amplification preserves positive trace-class block operators; for disjoint $B_n$ with union $B$, $J_B(T)=\sum_nJ_{B_n}(T)$ in trace norm for every trace-class $T$; and $J_X$ preserves trace. Its outcome effect $F_B$ is the unique effect with $\operatorname{tr}(J_B(T))=\operatorname{tr}(TF_B)$, its probability is $p(B)=\operatorname{tr}(J_B(\rho))$, and its conditional state is $J_B(\rho)/p(B)$ only when $p(B)>0$, as established in [[lem-nrqm-composites-general-trace-class-instrument-and-effect-duality]]. The Kraus case above is a concrete instance on $(A,2^A)$, with $J_B(T)=\sum_{a\in B,r}M_{a,r}TM_{a,r}^*$ in trace norm. This declaration does not assert that every abstract instrument has a Kraus representation or that a laboratory apparatus realizes it.

**(e) Declaration discipline.** A model of an apparatus that is used to predict post-measurement states must declare both an outcome structure (effects) and an update rule; the outcome law of P2 alone does not supply the update, and the update is not a mathematical consequence of the effects. The special case in which the Kraus family consists of the projections $P_{a}$ themselves (with a single $r$ per outcome) is the Lueders instrument of clauses (a)-(b). The claim that a concrete laboratory device realizes a particular declared measurement, filter or instrument is a physical identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 ([[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]), not a consequence of this definition.

**(f) Limits.** Declared ideal sharp measurements are idealizations of apparatus that are idealized as repeatable and projection-valued; the framework does not assert that every apparatus, or any particular apparatus, is of this form (clause (v) of P3). The following are outside the declared class and require their own models: a measurement of an exact value of a quantity whose spectrum is continuous (no normalization of a delta symbol is intended; clauses (iii) of P2 and (v) of P3); a photon-absorption or other destructive detector, whose declared instrument need not leave an outgoing state of the same form (clause (v) of P3); and a unitary system-apparatus interaction, which by itself produces conditional correlations without selecting a unique recorded outcome or a preferred outcome family (clause (v) of P3).

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) read P1, P2 and P3 in the measurement vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology of the page's later items; they add no assumption to those postulates. The cited mathematical items ([[lem-nrqm-measurement-selective-luders-update]], [[lem-nrqm-measurement-nonselective-luders-map]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-finite-effects-and-instruments]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-countable-kraus-normalization]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-general-trace-class-instrument-and-effect-duality]]) are conditional mathematics about the displayed formulas; no physical process, outcome uniqueness or empirical fact is deduced here.

**(a) Assigned sharp observables.** Adopt the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) for a declared system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned sharp observable** of the system is a pair $(A,u_A)$ consisting of a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ on the assigned Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) and a **declared unit** $u_A$ in which the real spectral coordinate of $A$ is read, in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. The domain $D(A)$ is part of the assignment: symmetry on a smaller domain, or a formal differential expression, does not by itself supply an assigned observable ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Whether a concrete laboratory quantity of a given apparatus is described by a particular pair $(A,u_A)$ is a tested identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 and is not produced by this definition.

**(b) Spectral measure and outcome law.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral suppliers. The self-adjoint operator $A$ has a unique spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$, with $D(A)=\{x:\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,x}<\infty\}$ and $Ax=\int\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)x$, where $E_{A,x}(B)=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$, that is a state $\rho\in D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], the **outcome law** of the pair $(A,u_A)$ in the preparation $\rho$ is the assignment
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_A(B)\bigr)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P2; for the pure preparation $[\psi]$ of a unit vector $\psi$ it is $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_A(B)\psi\|^{2}$, which depends only on the ray by [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. The law is a probability measure on the Borel sets by [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b), and it is affine in the preparation: for a statistical mixture $\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ one has $\mu^{A}_{\sum_nw_n\rho_n}=\sum_nw_n\mu^{A}_{\rho_n}$ by [[lem-nrqm-observables-outcome-law-affinity-and-trace-norm-continuity]] clause (b).

**(c) Outcome sets and exact values.** A declared finite-resolution outcome of the quantity is a Borel set $B$; its probability in the preparation $\rho$ is $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$, and a "value in $B$" is read only through this number. The reading of an **exact value** $\lambda$ is the singleton $B=\{\lambda\}$, with probability $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})$; by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-measure-atoms-and-eigenvalues]] clauses (a) and (b) this number is zero for every preparation unless $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, and when $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue it is the total weight of the eigenspace. In particular the model provides no normalizable eigenvector at a non-eigenvalue of $A$, and an exact value of a quantity with no eigenvalues is an idealization outside the assignment, in the sense of clause (iii) of P2.

**(d) Spectral support.** The outcomes of the observable lie in its spectrum: with $\sigma(A)$ the spectrum of [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]], one has $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))$ and $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$ for every preparation by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-support-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). This is the precise reading of the statement that the result of a measurement lies in the spectrum of the observable.

**(e) Moments.** The **mean** and the **variance** of the outcome law in a preparation are the numbers $\int\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ and $\int(\lambda-m)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ with $m$ the mean, read in the declared unit $u_A$ and its square respectively; they exist only under the integrability hypotheses of [[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]], which also supplies the formulas in terms of $A$ and the state. For a pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi\in D(A)$ the mean and the second moment are $\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$ and $\|A\psi\|^{2}$; membership of $\psi$ in $D(A)$ or in $D(A^{2})$ is a genuine hypothesis and is not asserted for an arbitrary preparation.

**(f) Unsharp finite outcomes are separate.** Clause (iv) of P2 permits a finite family of bounded effects $F_a$ with $0\le F_a\le I$ and $\sum_aF_a=I$ and outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$ as an operational description of a finite-resolution apparatus. That extension is tied to an apparatus instrument and is developed, together with state updates, on the measurement-and-instruments page; this definition fixes only the sharp outcome law of clause (b) and makes no claim that every laboratory procedure realizes it.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the spectral theorem, assert no dynamics, no joint measurement of several observables, no detector realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any physical system is exactly described by an assigned pair $(A,u_A)$. The additive additivity, support, atom and moment statements cited are mathematical consequences proved in the cited items; their physical reading is exactly the reading of P2 fixed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $E_{A,x}(B):=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ be its scalar measures ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ say that $\lambda$ is an **eigenvalue** of $A$ when $Ax=\lambda x$ for some nonzero $x\in D(A)$, the domain-restricted reading of [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]. Then:

(a) The orthogonal projection $E_A(\{\lambda\})$ is the projection of $H$ onto the eigenspace $\ker(A-\lambda)=\{x\in D(A):Ax=\lambda x\}$; in particular $E_A(\{\lambda\})\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.

(b) For every density operator $\rho$ on $H$, that is every self-adjoint positive trace-class $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)), the number $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(\{\lambda\}))$ is the weight that the scalar law $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ assigns to the singleton $\{\lambda\}$: it vanishes for every $\rho$ whenever $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, and it equals $1$ for the pure state $T_{u,u}$ of every unit eigenvector $u\in\ker(A-\lambda)$.

(c) If $A$ has no eigenvalues at all, then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=0$ for every density operator $\rho$ and every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$: the scalar law of every state carries no point mass, while its values on general Borel sets remain $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(B))$.

Clauses (a)-(c) are mathematical statements about $A$, $E_A$ and the density operators; no physical interpretation of $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ is asserted here.

Let $V$ be a two-dimensional complex inner product space with inner product
linear in the first argument ([[def-inner-product-space]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), and let $(e_{1},e_{2})$ be an
orthonormal basis of $V$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
For $\theta\in\mathbb R$ put
$$e_{\theta}:=\cos\theta\,e_{1}+\sin\theta\,e_{2},\qquad e_{\theta}^{\perp}:=-\sin\theta\,e_{1}+\cos\theta\,e_{2},$$
and for $x\in V$ define
$$P_{\theta}x:=\langle x,e_{\theta}\rangle\,e_{\theta},\qquad P_{\theta}^{\perp}x:=\langle x,e_{\theta}^{\perp}\rangle\,e_{\theta}^{\perp}.$$
Then:

(a) for every $\theta$ the maps $P_{\theta}$ and $P_{\theta}^{\perp}$ are
orthogonal projections on $V$ with ranges $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}$ and
$\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}$ ([[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]],
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]]), one has
$P_{\theta}+P_{\theta}^{\perp}=I$ and $P_{\theta}P_{\theta}^{\perp}=0$, and
$$P_{\theta}P_{\theta}=P_{\theta}=P_{\theta}^{*},\qquad P_{\theta}P_{\theta}^{\perp}=P_{\theta}^{\perp}P_{\theta}=0;$$

(b) for all real $\varphi,\theta$ the unit vectors
$\psi_{\varphi}:=\cos\varphi\,e_{1}+\sin\varphi\,e_{2}$ satisfy
$$\langle e_{\theta},\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\cos(\theta-\varphi),\qquad \langle\psi_{\varphi},P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\|P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=|\langle e_{\theta},\psi_{\varphi}\rangle|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi),$$
and $\langle\psi_{\varphi},P_{\theta}^{\perp}\psi_{\varphi}\rangle=\sin^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$;

(c) the assignments $\theta\mapsto P_{\theta}$ and $\theta\mapsto
P_{\theta}^{\perp}$ are $2\pi$-periodic, $P_{\theta+\pi}=P_{\theta}$ and
$P_{\theta+\pi/2}=P_{\theta}^{\perp}$, and for every $z\in\mathbb C$ and
$x\in V$ one has $P_{\theta}(zx)=zP_{\theta}x$ and
$\|P_{\theta}(z\psi_{\varphi})\|^{2}/\|z\psi_{\varphi}\|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$
whenever $z\ne0$; in particular the number $\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$ depends
only on the ray $[\psi_{\varphi}]$, not on the representative;

(d) the pair $(P_{\theta},P_{\theta}^{\perp})$ is a two-element family of
mutually orthogonal projections on $V$ with $P_{\theta}+P_{\theta}^{\perp}=I$,
the spectral values $1$ and $0$ of the bounded self-adjoint operator
$P_{\theta}$ have projections $P_{\theta}$ and $P_{\theta}^{\perp}$,
respectively. These two alternatives may be labelled $+1$ and $-1$ in a
declared analyser; those labels are not the spectral values of $P_{\theta}$.
The eigenspace of $P_{\theta}$ at eigenvalue $1$ is
$\mathbb Ce_{\theta}$ and the eigenspace at eigenvalue $0$ is
$\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}$.

No physical interpretation of $V$, of the pair $(e_{1},e_{2})$ or of the
projections $P_{\theta}$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). For a self-adjoint trace-class operator $T$ on $H$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]) and a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ put
$$\Phi_T(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(TE_A(B)\bigr)\in\mathbb C .$$
Then:

(a) $|\Phi_T(B)|\le\|T\|_1$ for every Borel set $B$; the map $T\mapsto\Phi_T(B)$ is real-linear on the self-adjoint trace-class operators; and for every density operator $\rho$ one has $0\le\Phi_\rho(B)\le1$, so that $\mu^{A}_\rho:=\Phi_\rho$ is a probability measure on the Borel sets with $\mu^{A}_\rho(\mathbb R)=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b)).

(b) If $\rho=\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ is a statistical mixture of density operators $\rho_n$ with weights $w_n\ge0$, $\sum_nw_n=1$, the trace-norm convergent sum of [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-density-set-convex-and-complete]], then for every Borel set $B$
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\sum_nw_n\,\mu^{A}_{\rho_n}(B),$$
the series converging absolutely.

(c) For density operators $\rho,\sigma$ one has
$$\sup\{\,|\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)-\mu^{A}_{\sigma}(B)|:\ B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}\,\}\le\|\rho-\sigma\|_1,$$
and if density operators $\rho_k$ converge to $\rho$ in trace norm, then $\mu^{A}_{\rho_k}(B)\to\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$ uniformly over all Borel sets $B$.

**Density operators.** Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space. A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a) ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). The **state space** of $H$ is the set of all density operators on $H$ and is denoted
$$D(H):=\{\rho:\rho\ \text{is a density operator on}\ H\}.$$
An element of $D(H)$ is called a **state** of $H$ in the mathematical sense fixed here.

**Pure states.** A state $\rho\in D(H)$ is **pure** when there is a unit vector $u\in S(H)$ with
$$\rho=T_{u,u},\qquad T_{u,u}x=\langle x,u\rangle u\quad(x\in H),$$
where $T_{u,u}$ is the rank-one operator of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] and $S(H)$ is the unit sphere of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. By [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] the pure states are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range, and the map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow D(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
on the ray space $R(H)$, with $\nu$ the normalization map, is well defined and injective with image the set of pure states. A state is **mixed** when it is not pure. For a nonzero vector $\psi$ the **normalized rank-one operator of $\psi$** is
$$\widehat\rho(\psi):=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})},$$
which equals $T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)}$; thus $\widehat\rho(\psi)$ is the pure state of the ray $[\psi]$, and the vector $\psi$ enters only through its ray.

**Purity.** For $\rho\in D(H)$ the operator $\rho^{2}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class: it is self-adjoint by the adjoint algebra of [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], positive because $\langle\rho^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle\rho x,\rho x\rangle\ge0$, and trace class because $\rho$ is a bounded trace-class operator and the trace-class operators form a two-sided ideal ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]] clauses 1 and 2). The **purity** of $\rho$ is the real number
$$\mathcal P(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})\in\mathbb R.$$
The numerical range of the purity and the equivalence of purity with purity of the state are established by the purity criterion of this page; this definition records the object only.

**Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical state space of a Hilbert space together with the pure states, the mixed states, the normalized rank-one operator of a nonzero vector and the purity functional. The cited rank-one calculus and the density-operator expansion assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and the definition is read under that assumption. It asserts no dynamics, no measurement, no probability law and no physical interpretation, and it introduces no new assumptions beyond the cited mathematics and that choice hypothesis. In particular, whether a given physical preparation is described by a pure or a mixed state is a question about the model's assignments, not about this definition.

derivations.claim: [The analyser is a declared ideal sharp measurement] By [F1] the two projections of the analyser are bounded, orthogonal and mutually orthogonal with $P_{\theta}+P_{\theta}^{\perp}=I$; therefore the pair $(P_{\theta},P_{\theta}^{\perp})$ is a declared ideal sharp measurement in the sense of clause (a) of the measurement definition, with outcome labels $+1$ and $-1$. This is (a).

[Spectral law] The operator $P_{\theta}$ is bounded and self-adjoint by [F1], so it has a spectral projection-valued measure $E$ ([[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b)). Its eigenvalues are $1$ and $0$, with eigenspaces $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}$ and $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}$ by [F1]; by [F3], $E(\{1\})$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}$, that is $P_{\theta}$, and $E(\{0\})$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathbb Ce_{\theta}^{\perp}$, that is $P_{\theta}^{\perp}=I-P_{\theta}$. Since $P_{\theta}$ is a projection one has $P_{\theta}^2=P_{\theta}$, so for $\lambda\notin\{0,1\}$ the bounded operator $\frac{1}{1-\lambda}P_{\theta}-\frac{1}{\lambda}(I-P_{\theta})$ is a two-sided inverse of $P_{\theta}-\lambda I$ (multiplying out gives $P_{\theta}+(I-P_{\theta})=I$), hence the spectrum is contained in $\{0,1\}$ ([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]], [[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]); therefore $E(\mathbb R\setminus\{0,1\})=E(\mathbb R\setminus\sigma(P_{\theta}))=0$ by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-support-and-outcome-law]] clause (a). For any preparation $\rho$ the outcome law of the assigned quantity $P_{\theta}$ at the value $1$ is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(\{1\}))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_{\theta})$ by [F2]; the analyser label $-1$ corresponds to the quantity's spectral value $0$, whose projection is $E(\{0\})=P_{\theta}^{\perp}$, and the two weights sum to $\operatorname{tr}(\rho I)=1$. This is (b).

[Pure preparations] Let $\psi=\alpha e_{1}+\beta e_{2}$ be a unit vector. Since $E(\{1\})=P_{\theta}$, the probability is $\|P_{\theta}\psi\|^{2}=\langle\psi,P_{\theta}\psi\rangle=|\langle\psi,e_{\theta}\rangle|^{2}=|\alpha\cos\theta+\beta\sin\theta|^{2}$; for $\psi=\psi_{\varphi}$ this equals $\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$ by [F4], and then $p_{-1}=1-p_{+1}=\sin^{2}(\theta-\varphi)$.

[Mixtures and phases] If $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ is a statistical mixture, [F5] gives $p_{+1}(\rho)=\sum_{n}w_{n}\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{n}P_{\theta})=\sum_{n}w_{n}p_{+1}(\rho_{n})$. The number $|\langle z\psi,e_{\theta}\rangle|^{2}/\|z\psi\|^{2}=|\langle\psi,e_{\theta}\rangle|^{2}$ for $z\ne0$ is unchanged by scaling the representative, so the law depends only on the rays; the identities $P_{\theta+2\pi}=P_{\theta}$ and $P_{\theta+\pi}=P_{\theta}$ of [F4] give the stated periodicities, and $p_{+1}(\theta,\varphi)=\cos^{2}(\theta-\varphi)=p_{+1}(\theta-\varphi,0)$. This proves (c) and (d).

[Conditional and discarded states] Let $\rho$ be a preparation with $p_{+1}(\rho)>0$. By [F5] the conditional state after the outcome $+1$ is $\rho_{+1}=P_{\theta}\rho P_{\theta}/p_{+1}(\rho)$. For the pure preparation of $\psi_{\varphi}$ with $\cos(\theta-\varphi)\ne0$ one has $P_{\theta}\psi_{\varphi}=\langle\psi_{\varphi},e_{\theta}\rangle e_{\theta}=\cos(\theta-\varphi)e_{\theta}$ by [F4]; hence $P_{\theta}\rho P_{\theta}=|\cos(\theta-\varphi)|^{2}T_{e_{\theta},e_{\theta}}$ and $\rho_{+1}=T_{e_{\theta},e_{\theta}}$, the pure state of the ray $[e_{\theta}]$ ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]). Applying the pure-preparation formula of step 1.3 to the preparation $[e_{\theta}]$ at analyser angle $\theta'$ gives conditional probability $|\langle e_{\theta},e_{\theta'}\rangle|^{2}=\cos^{2}(\theta'-\theta)$ by [F4]. The discarded-outcome state is $\Phi(\rho)=P_{\theta}\rho P_{\theta}+P_{\theta}^{\perp}\rho P_{\theta}^{\perp}$ by [F5]. This proves (e).

[Assembly and scope] Steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove (a) and (b), steps 1.3 and 1.4 prove (c) and (d), and step 2.1 proves (e). All assertions are conditional on P1, P2, P3 and the adopted model; no laboratory apparatus, no sampling model and no measured number occurs in the argument, which is (f).

complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers

$\|\Pi_n\psi\|=\|\psi_n\|$ and $\|\Pi_n\|\le1$; it satisfies
$\Pi_n^2=\Pi_n$, $\Pi_n^*=\Pi_n$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]), and
